name: Aaron Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at Ledgerline, a payroll software company with about 300 people, and I'm on the team that keeps the old billing module alive. It's mostly PHP, which is an older web language, and a lot of my day is fixing small bugs that customers report and writing tests for them. I'm at my desk by nine, there's a ten-minute stand-up meeting, then I pick a ticket and grind on it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a bug finally makes sense, when you trace it back and it's one wrong line. What wears me out is that I'm slower than the others, and my last review literally said I need to improve my speed. Marcus, the senior guy I eat lunch with, says I'm careful, which is nice, but careful isn't what gets counted. And I don't use the AI coding assistant the company bought, which some people think is the reason I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd say 'told you so' in the team chat, maybe with a gif. I've been the guy saying it's mostly hype since the company rolled out the assistant last spring. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone to people instead of chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a flat AI world doesn't fix my problem, which is that I'm the slowest one on my team. The routine stuff it does automate is exactly my kind of work, like writing tests and small fixes. So I'd still feel like I'm one bad review away from being shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, but I'd actually take Marcus up on his offer to pair with me on Thursdays so I get faster. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe 150, because rent went up again in March. And I'd keep going to the tech workers' meetups about forming a union, which I've been half-attending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not off the hook. It's like dodging a storm and then remembering the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the review. What did it actually say, and how did it land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It said 'meets most expectations, needs to improve velocity', velocity meaning how many tickets you close. My manager Lin said it isn't a warning, but I read it about twenty times on the bus home. Dana, my girlfriend, told me to stop rereading it and go to bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you half-attend the union meetups. What keeps you at half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, a bit. Ledgerline isn't anti-union on paper, but nobody wants to be the junior with the slow review who's also the one handing out union cards. If the guy with the weakest review leads the union drive, management sees an easy target.

say: I'd tell my team **told you so**, because I've called the AI assistant hype since spring.
I'd post that the money should have gone to **people**, not chatbots.
think: A flat AI world doesn't fix my real problem: I'm the **slowest** on my team.
The **routine work** it does automate, like tests and small fixes, is exactly what I do.
do: Start **pairing with Marcus** every Thursday to get faster at closing tickets.
Keep saving about **150 a month**, since rent went up again in March.
Keep going to the **union meetups**, though only halfway for now.
feel: **Relieved** that the big change doesn't come, but still worried about his place on the team.
S0.quote: If the guy with the weakest review leads the union drive, management sees an easy target.
fieldNote: His worry here comes from a **weak review**, not from AI, so a quiet AI world barely helps.
He refuses the **AI assistant** on principle, and suspects colleagues blame his slowness on that.
Wants a union but is held back by **fear** of being singled out.

steps.text: Pair with Marcus every Thursday to close tickets faster
Put 150 a month into savings despite the rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a union now, not next year, and I'd say it out loud at lunch. Online I'd share every story about juniors being let go while the company brags about AI. I'd say the bosses are using the robots, I mean the software, as an excuse to cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm exactly the kind of person who gets cut. Junior, slow, and the one guy who won't touch the assistant. When they decide the team needs four people instead of six, my name is the obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sign the union card and ask Marcus and two others to sign too. I'd move my savings from about three months to as close to six as I can, so an extra 250 a month, and Dana and I would skip the trip to her sister's wedding abroad. If they made the assistant mandatory, I'd use it, but only for the boring tests, and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It's that feeling when your name is on a list you can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the assistant if forced. Why not start now, before they force you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's trained on other people's code that nobody asked permission for, and that still bothers me. And I learn by typing it myself; if it writes it, I don't understand it. I know that sounds like a reason to get fired, and maybe it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemi, who started three months after me, because she's on a work visa and losing the job means leaving the country. And the support team downstairs, because answering customers is right there on the list. Honestly, they'd go before me.

say: I'd say at lunch that we need a **union now**, not next year.
I'd post that bosses use the **software as an excuse** to cut people.
think: I'm exactly the one who gets **cut**: junior, slow and refusing the assistant.
When they want four people instead of six, my **name** is the obvious one.
do: Sign the **union card** in the first month and ask Marcus and two others to sign.
Save an extra **250 a month** and skip the trip to Dana's sister's wedding abroad.
Use the assistant **only if forced**, and only for the boring tests.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of being on a layoff list he can't see.
S1.quote: I'm exactly the kind of person who gets cut. Junior, slow, and the one guy who won't touch the assistant.
fieldNote: He openly expects to be the **first cut**, which makes this alarmed even though he's acting calmly.
His refusal of AI is **moral and practical**: stolen code, and fear of not understanding his own work.
Thinks of **colleagues** first, like Kemi on a work visa and the support team.

steps.text: Sign the union card and get Marcus and two others to sign
Save an extra 250 a month and skip the wedding trip abroad
Use the AI assistant only for tests if management makes it mandatory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest theft of work in history, and the government has to step in with a basic income or something like it. I'd be at every protest I could get to. At work I'd say there's no point pretending, we're all training our replacements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I'm done as a developer by 2028, probably before. I'd have under two years, three months of savings and a diploma for a job that doesn't exist anymore. The only reason I'm not completely lost is Dana, because she's a nurse and robots are years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up with the tech workers' union and actually run the meetups instead of half-attending. We'd cut hard: sell my car, cancel the gym and the streaming stuff, and live on Dana's pay so mine goes into savings. And I'd write to my representative every month about a basic income, because one letter changes nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry underneath the scared. I'd feel stupid for picking this career three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dana the night you realised this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd say sorry first, which is weird because it's not my fault. Then I'd ask if she'd be okay carrying us for a while. She works night shifts on a hospital ward, and she'd probably say we'll manage, and I'd lie awake anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are years behind for Dana. What happens around 2031, when they arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I hate that I don't know. Maybe nursing lasts longer because people want a human holding their hand. But if both of us are out by 2031, then I'm not worried about my job anymore, I'm worried about rent and everything.

say: I'd call it the biggest **theft** of work in history and demand a **basic income**.
I'd tell my team we're all **training our replacements**.
think: I'm **done as a developer** by 2028, with three months of savings.
Only **Dana's nursing job** keeps us going, because robots come about three years later.
do: Run the **union meetups** instead of half-attending them.
Sell **the car**, cancel the gym and streaming, and live on Dana's pay.
Write to his **representative** every month about a basic income.
feel: Feels stupid for choosing **this career** three years ago.
S2.quote: I'd feel stupid for picking this career three years ago.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his job outright; his **girlfriend's income** is the only thing keeping this short of panic.
The three-year robot gap matters to him through **Dana's nursing**, not his own work.
Blames **AI firms and bosses**, and wants government to step in.

steps.text: Run the tech workers' union meetups every month
Sell the car and cancel the gym and streaming services
Write to his representative monthly about a basic income
Live on Dana's nursing pay and save his own salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get rules in place, like notice periods and paying people while they retrain. I'd say it calmly at work so people actually listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds like a lot, but I know myself. I'd tell myself I'll make a plan next year, and then it would be 2030. I'm still the junior who goes first, just a bit later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job as long as they'll have me and push hard for the union, because a contract with severance pay matters more with five years to win it. I'd save toward six months of expenses. And I'd look at an IT job at Dana's hospital, because hospitals are slow to change everything, even with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more of a slow dread. Like knowing your lease ends and you haven't looked for a new place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hospitals are slow to change. What's the hospital job, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an IT team that keeps the patient records system running, and Dana knows one of the guys. It's not glamorous, mostly fixing printers and access problems, and it pays a bit less. But that kind of job needs a person walking to a ward, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself to plan next year. What would actually make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably seeing someone like me get cut. If Kemi or another junior went, that's when I'd move. I'm not proud of that, but I don't move until I'm pushed.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to win rules like notice periods and paid retraining.
I'd say it **calmly** at work so people actually listen.
think: Five years feels long, but I'd **put off** making a plan until 2030.
I'm still the **junior who goes first**, just a bit later.
do: Push the **union** for a contract with **severance pay** while there's time.
Ask about the **hospital IT team** where Dana works.
feel: A **slow dread**, like a lease ending with nowhere lined up.
S3.quote: I don't move until I'm pushed.
fieldNote: He's honest that **extra time** may not help, because he waits until forced.
Looks for **hands-on** corners of IT, like walking to hospital wards, to buy time.
The **severance contract** is his main hope, not personal change.

steps.text: Push the union for a contract with severance pay
Build savings to six months of expenses
Ask about an IT job at Dana's hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say this is a choice, not a disaster. Governments and companies can plan this properly, so I'd push for paid retraining and a shorter working week. I'd post that we've got a decade, so nobody gets to say they were surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd want to be out of software well before then. Ten years is enough to train for something with my hands, even for someone slow like me. Robots come around 2039, so a hands-on job buys me a few more years again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in my second or third year, maybe as an electrician, because my uncle did that and never ran out of work. I'd keep the Ledgerline job to pay for it. And I'd keep pushing the union and voting for whoever promises paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, almost okay. Still tight in my chest, but it feels like something I can walk through instead of fall off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're slow to change. Would you really start a course in year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe year three, if I'm honest. Dana would nag me, and she'd be right. I just know I'd need someone to sign me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician and not something closer to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because anything closer to software is the stuff AGI eats first. Wiring a house still needs someone in the loft with a torch, at least until 2039. And I like the idea of fixing something you can actually touch.

say: I'd say with **ten years** this is a choice, not a disaster.
I'd push for **paid retraining** and a **shorter week**, and say nobody gets to act surprised.
think: I'd be **37** when it lands and want to be out of software before then.
A **hands-on** job buys me a few more years, until robots around 2039.
do: Start a **part-time electrician course** in year two or three.
Keep the **Ledgerline job** to pay for the course.
Keep backing the union and **vote** for paid retraining.
feel: **Almost okay**, still tight in the chest but able to walk through it.
S4.quote: Wiring a house still needs someone in the loft with a torch, at least until 2039.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his dread into a **plan**, though he admits he'd need a push to start.
He uses the **robot gap** directly, choosing electrical work over anything near software.
Still expects to **lose** the developer job, so anxious rather than calm.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time electrician course by year three
Keep the Ledgerline job to pay for the course
Vote for candidates who promise paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have no time and I'm not a fast mover. What would help is a union contract that gives real notice and a year of pay, and public money so I can retrain while still paying rent. I never let a machine write my code, and a machine is still the thing that takes my job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who decided this was fine. Nobody asked people like me or Kemi, and that's the part that makes me angriest.

headlineQuote: I never let a machine write my code, and a machine is still the thing that takes my job.
portrait: A **27-year-old junior developer** maintaining old billing code at a payroll software firm, living with his nurse girlfriend Dana.
Refuses the **AI assistant** on principle and fears his slowness makes him the first to go.
Progressive and **pro-union**, but scared to lead because of his weak review.
Moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the fast scenarios.
Only with **ten years** does he picture retraining as an electrician.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time and admits he's a slow mover.
whatWouldHelp: A **union contract** with real notice and a year of pay.
**Public money** to retrain while still paying rent.
